### Hydrogen – A Quick Reference Guide | Property | Value / Description | Notes | |----------|---------------------|-------| | **Chemical Symbol** | H | | | **Atomic Number** | 1 | Only one proton in the nucleus. | | **Atomic Mass** | ~1.008 u (average) | Weighted average of its naturally occurring isotopes. | | **Isotopes** | • **¹H** (protium) – 99.98 % natural abundance
• **²H** (deuterium) – 0.02 % natural abundance
• **³H** (tritium) – trace amounts, radioactive (half‑life ≈ 12.32 yr) | Deuterium is used in heavy water; tritium in nuclear fusion research. | | **Electron Configuration** | 1s¹ | One valence electron. | | **Electronegativity (Pauling)** | 2.20 | Highest among all elements. | | **First Ionization Energy** | 13.598 eV | Energy required to remove the single valence electron. | | **Electron Affinity** | –0.754 eV | Slightly negative, indicating a weak tendency to gain an electron. | | **Molecular Formula** | H₂ (diatomic) | The most stable form under normal conditions. | | **Molecular Weight** | 2.016 g mol⁻¹ | For H₂. | | **Boiling Point** | –252.87 °C (20.28 K) | Extremely low; boils at ~20 K. | | **Melting Point** | –259.16 °C (14.01 K) | Freezes at ~14 K. | | **Density at STP** | 0.08988 g L⁻¹ | Very light; lighter than air. | | **Color** | Colorless | | | **Odor** | Odorless | | | **Taste** | Tasteless | | | **State at Room Temperature** | Gas | | | **Solubility in Water** | ~1.6 g L⁻¹ (at 25 °C) | Slightly soluble; forms hydronium ions when dissolved. | | **Flammability** | Highly flammable | Forms explosive mixtures with air (1–4 % H₂ in air). | | **Reactivity** | Very reactive with halogens, oxygen, and many metals | Forms hydrides (e.g., NaH, CaH₂). | | **Acidity/Basicity** | Acts as a very strong acid in aqueous solution (forms H₃O⁺) | In non‑aqueous solvents, it behaves as a weak base (forming H₂). | | **Spectral Lines** | Lyman series (UV), Balmer series (visible) | Classic hydrogen emission spectrum. | | **Role in Biology** | Essential for life; part of water, organic molecules, ATP, etc. | | | **Industrial Uses** | Fuel (hydrogen fuel cells), ammonia synthesis (Haber process), petroleum refining, metal processing | | | **Energy Density** | 120 MJ kg⁻¹ (by mass) | Highest among fuels; lower by volume compared to hydrocarbons. | | **Safety Concerns** | Explosive mixtures, cryogenic hazards, tritium radioactivity | Requires careful handling and storage. | #### Key Takeaways 1. **Hydrogen is the simplest element** – one proton, one electron, and a single stable isotope (protium) that dominates natural abundance. 2. **It exists almost exclusively as a diatomic gas (H₂)** under standard conditions, but can form various compounds (hydrides, acids, bases). 3. **Its physical properties are extreme**: very low boiling/melting points, high flammability, and a very low density. 4. **Chemically, it is highly reactive** due to its lone valence electron and high electronegativity, making it a powerful oxidizing agent and a key building block in organic chemistry. 5. **Hydrogen’s isotopes** (deuterium and tritium) have important scientific and industrial applications, especially in nuclear fusion research and as tracers in biochemical studies. Feel free to ask if you’d like deeper details on any specific property or application!
